subsystems.name: Cell source and expansion
subsystems.role: supplies the patient's own cells so the printed organ is not rejected.
parts: directed differentiation into organ-specific cell types

subsystems.name: Bio-ink formulation
subsystems.role: turns cells into a printable material that keeps them alive.
parts: hydrogel base (alginate, gelatin, hyaluronic acid derivatives)

subsystems.name: Bioprinter
subsystems.role: deposits ink precisely, layer by layer, into an organ-shaped geometry.
parts: extrusion, inkjet or laser-assisted print heads

subsystems.name: Vascular network
subsystems.role: gives every cell a blood supply within a fraction of a millimetre.
parts: sacrificial filaments that are dissolved out

subsystems.name: Maturation bioreactor
subsystems.role: perfuses and conditions the construct until cells organise into working tissue.
parts: mechanical or electrical conditioning for muscle and heart

subsystems.name: Implantation and monitoring
subsystems.role: connects the organ to the patient and tracks how it takes.
parts: surgical anastomosis to host vessels and ducts

buildSteps.title: Harvest and reprogram cells
buildSteps.detail: A small biopsy or blood sample is taken; the cells are reprogrammed into iPSCs and grown up in large numbers.

buildSteps.title: Differentiate the cells
buildSteps.detail: Chemical and genetic cues steer the stem cells into the several cell types a whole organ needs — not just one.

buildSteps.title: Design the blueprint
buildSteps.detail: CT or MRI scans of the patient define the organ's size and shape; software converts that into a print path including the branching vessel tree.

buildSteps.title: Formulate the bio-inks
buildSteps.detail: Cell-laden hydrogels are mixed to a printable viscosity, alongside a sacrificial ink that will later be washed out to leave channels.

buildSteps.title: Print the construct
buildSteps.detail: The printer lays down tens of thousands of droplets or filaments into a support bath that holds soft shapes upright — the scaffold-free approach relies on the support medium rather than a permanent plastic frame.

buildSteps.title: Build the vasculature
buildSteps.detail: Channels are printed from the largest artery down to a capillary-scale network; the sacrificial ink is dissolved and endothelial cells are flowed in to line them.

buildSteps.title: Mature in a bioreactor
buildSteps.detail: The construct is perfused for days to weeks so cells self-organise, lay down their own matrix and start performing organ-specific functions.

buildSteps.title: Test before implant
buildSteps.detail: Function, sterility and the absence of unwanted cell types are checked; because the cells are the patient's own, rejection risk is low.

buildSteps.title: Implant and follow up
buildSteps.detail: The organ is surgically connected to the patient's blood supply and, where relevant, ducts — then monitored as it integrates.

prerequisites.why: they give an unlimited, patient-matched cell source instead of scarce donor cells.
printing several cell types and fine channels at once is demonstrated but not yet at organ scale.
no printed tissue much thicker than about a millimetre survives, because diffusion alone cannot feed its cells.
tissues must be grown to functional maturity outside the body before implantation.

prerequisites.tech: Regulatory and manufacturing standards for living implants
prerequisites.why: cell-therapy rules exist, but whole personalised organs fit no established approval route.

pathway.milestone: lab-grown organoids, skin, cartilage and small tissue patches; simple engineered bladders were implanted in patients in the 2000s
pathway.unlocks: proof that printed and engineered tissue can survive in the body.

pathway.milestone: thick, fully vascularised tissue patches for heart and kidney, tested in animals and early human safety trials
pathway.unlocks: solving the blood-supply problem that blocks every solid organ.

pathway.milestone: first whole printed organs with simple structure, such as a kidney subunit or bladder, used in a small number of patients
pathway.unlocks: clinical and regulatory pathways for personalised living implants.

pathway.milestone: hospital-scale on-demand printing from a stored cell sample
pathway.unlocks: replacement organs without waiting lists or lifelong anti-rejection drugs.
